detail.question: What does Mill claim about the abilities of women who have ruled as queens or regents?
detail.answer: Mill claims that women who have ruled have shown real ability, and that this is a matter of fact rather than inference. He says it is "quite certain" that a woman can be a Queen Elizabeth, a Deborah, or a Joan of Arc (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Reigning queens are far fewer than kings, but a far larger proportion of them have shown talents for rule. Many of them reigned in difficult periods. They were often marked by firmness and vigour as well as intelligence, which is the opposite of the conventional picture of women's character. Adding regents and viceroys of provinces makes the list of eminent women rulers very long (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). In a note, he reports from his long official knowledge of Hindoo governments that well-governed principalities were, in three cases out of four, under a woman's rule. These women acted as legal regents during an heir's minority. He calls this a very striking example of women's natural capacity for government (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Note footnote_2_1 to Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). He also argues that most great queens were great through their own talents for government and kept the supreme direction of affairs in their own hands. In his view, listening to good advisers shows good judgment (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). As evidence that women govern well even when not sovereign, he cites Margaret of Austria, a governor of the Netherlands under Charles the Fifth, as one of the ablest politicians of her age (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). Finally, he says that where women's capacities for government have been tried, in that proportion they have been found adequate. He attributes this to princesses having been allowed the same range of interests and freedom of development as men (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: The passages do not use one single named metaphor for the limits of pure understanding, but the closest image is that of an "empty space." Kant says the representation of a noumenon (an object thought only non-sensuously) is for us "quite void." It serves only to mark the limits of our sensuous intuition, leaving "an empty space" that we cannot fill by means of either possible experience or the pure understanding (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Appendix, paragraph 27 (edition-specific)). A related image appears elsewhere: when the pure conceptions of the understanding are extended beyond our intuition, they are "mere empty conceptions of objects." Kant also says they are "mere forms of thought, without objective reality" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §19, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He likewise says that a mode of determining an object by mere thought is only "a logical form without content" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Appendix, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)). Kant also draws a spatial analogy: the limits of the understanding's conceptions are determined "just as" the transcendental aesthetic determined the limits of our pure form of sensuous intuition (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §19, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Strictly speaking, these are images of emptiness and boundary, not an elaborated metaphor, and the passages do not name a single metaphor.

detail.answer:
Kant gives the understanding the role of uniting the manifold (the variety) in our representations. Several passages support this.

1. Combination is the understanding's own act. Kant says it is "an operation of the understanding itself," and he describes the understanding as the faculty of conjoining a priori and of bringing the variety of given representations under the unity of apperception (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §12, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). The same passage calls this principle the highest in all human cognition.

2. Unity of consciousness is the condition of union. An object is that in whose conception the manifold of a given intuition is united. All union of representations requires unity of consciousness in their synthesis, and this unity is what makes representations relate to an object and become cognitions (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §13, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). Kant also says the synthetical unity of apperception is the highest point with which every operation of the understanding must be connected, and that this faculty is the understanding itself (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Note block 155 to Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §12, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

3. The understanding works together with the imagination. Synthesis of representations rests on the imagination, while their synthetical unity, which a judgement requires, rests on the unity of apperception (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book II, Chapter 2, Section II, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). For cognition of an object, the diversity of pure intuition is given first. The imagination's synthesis of it comes second, but this gives no cognition yet. Third come the conceptions that give unity to this pure synthesis, and these are given by the understanding (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)).

4. The same function unifies judgements and intuitions. Kant defines "function" as the unity of the act of arranging diverse representations under one common representation. He says judgements are functions of unity in our representations (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §4, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The same function that unifies different representations in a judgement also unifies the mere synthesis of different representations in an intuition. This unity is called the pure conception of the understanding (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 1, §6, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What criticism does Hume make of philosophers who claim that all power belongs directly to God?

top_retrieved.author: Immanuel Kant
top_retrieved.locator: Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 35 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Hume's criticism is that these philosophers (the occasionalists, who hold that apparent natural causes are only "occasions" for God's direct volition) undermine the very greatness they want to honor. He describes their view: they treat mind and intelligence as "the immediate and sole cause of every event" in nature, so that objects commonly called causes are only occasions, and God himself moves the second billiard-ball (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §55, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). They extend this to the union of soul and body and to the will's power over bodily motion (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §55, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

Hume says they "rob nature, and all created beings, of every power" in order to make dependence on the Deity "still more sensible and immediate" (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §56, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). But he argues that, by this theory, they "diminish, instead of magnifying, the grandeur" of the divine attributes they celebrate (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §56, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). His reasons: it shows more power in God to delegate some power to creatures than to produce everything by immediate volition. It also shows more wisdom to design the world at the start with such foresight that it serves providence by its own operation, than to have the Creator adjust its parts and animate all its wheels at every moment (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VII, Part I, §56, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Wollstonecraft says children should not be taught to make allowances for their parents' faults. She argues that every such allowance weakens the force of reason in their minds and makes them more indulgent to their own faults (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). She presents this as a dilemma for an instructor: teaching virtue on any solid principle amounts to teaching children to despise their parents (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). She calls being severe with oneself and forbearing to others one of the most sublime virtues of maturity. Children, in her view, should be taught only the simple virtues (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). If they start too early to make allowance for human passions and manners, they wear off the fine edge of the criterion by which they should regulate their own conduct. They become unjust in the same proportion as they grow indulgent (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 11, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Hobbes lists four abuses of speech, and the first is the one that deceives the speaker himself. It happens when men "register their thoughts wrong, by the inconstancy of the signification of their words", that is, when the meanings of their words shift. They then record as their conceptions something they never actually conceived, and so deceive themselves (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). By contrast, Hobbes says the second abuse, using words metaphorically (in a sense other than the one they were ordained for), deceives others rather than oneself (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

A related warning appears elsewhere. Hobbes says it is fallacious to judge the nature of things by the ordinary and inconstant use of words. His example is that "Doe this" can express a command, counsel, or exhortation, and people who ignore the circumstances mistake one for another (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 25, Counsell What, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The passage ties this confusion to whatever suits the conclusions they want to draw, but it does not explicitly call it self-deception.

detail.answer:
Wollstonecraft attacks these arguments on several grounds. The passages show her doing so in the following ways.

1. She points out the flaw in the reasoning. She describes the argument she opposes as holding that women should be weak and passive because they have less bodily strength, and that they were therefore formed to please and be subject to man, with their duty being to make themselves agreeable to their "master" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §1, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). She replies that even if woman were proved naturally weaker, it would not follow that she should labour to become weaker than nature intended. She calls such arguments "an insult to common sense" that "savour of passion" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 3, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

2. She challenges husbandly authority directly. She compares the "divine right of husbands" to the divine right of kings. She says that in an enlightened age it may be contested "without danger" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 3, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). She also quotes a writer who teaches that a woman should learn to suffer injustice and bear a husband's insults without complaint (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §1, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). Her response to that teaching in these passages is the broader argument that duty needs reason behind it, as described in points 3 and 5.

3. She argues that women's weakness harms the very duties it is meant to serve. She asks whether "passive indolent women make the best wives". She doubts that women who have absorbed notions of passive obedience have enough character to manage a family or educate children (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 2, paragraph 62 (edition-specific)). She says that educating children and running a family require understanding and strength of body and mind. She accuses the men who want to domesticate women of trying to weaken their bodies and cramp their minds (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)). She concludes that "reason is absolutely necessary to enable a woman to perform any duty properly", and that sensibility is not reason (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 4, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)).

4. She links the demand for weakness to tyranny and slavery. She compares such arguments to those of tyrants who crush reason while claiming to be useful. She asks whether a duty can be binding if it is not founded on reason. She says that without understanding no authority can make women do their duty virtuously, and that women kept in this state may be "convenient slaves" while slavery degrades both master and dependent (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Dedication, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

5. She ties duty to rights. Women are made slaves to their persons and must govern their "tyrants" by sinister tricks, because "without rights there cannot be any incumbent duties". She adds that the laws treat a man and wife as a unit and consider only him responsible, reducing her to a "mere cypher" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 9, paragraph 15 (edition-specific)).

The Mill passage supplied does not bear on Wollstonecraft's own argument, so I have not used it.

detail.answer:
Wollstonecraft's main test is whether a reason can be given. She says a prejudice is "a fond obstinate persuasion" for which we can give no reason. The moment a reason can be given for an opinion, it "ceases to be a prejudice, though it may be an error in judgment" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)). So an opinion backed by reason can still be wrong, but it is not a prejudice. A prejudice is held without a reason, or without one that can be traced.

She also explains how opinions turn into prejudices. In her account, opinions of every kind were probably first considered and so rested on some reason, though sometimes that reason was a local expedient rather than a lasting principle. They become prejudices when they are "indolently adopted" only because age has given them a venerable look, even though the reason they were built on has ceased to be a reason or can no longer be traced (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)).

She adds that people often use reason to defend prejudices rather than to examine them. Men, she says, seem to employ their reason to justify prejudices they have absorbed without knowing how, rather than to root them out. She describes this as a kind of intellectual cowardice, since forming one's own principles takes a strong mind (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). Cherishing an opinion simply because one holds it, she says, resembles what is "vulgarly termed a woman's reason" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §5, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)).

The passages say nothing more about how to judge whether a given reason is sound.

detail.answer: Smith says that when great landowners spend their rents on tenants and retainers, each landowner wholly maintains his own tenants and retainers (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Such tenants and retainers are dependent on him. A tenant at will, a tenant who holds land at the owner's pleasure, is described as being as dependent as any servant or retainer. The landowner feeds his tenants at their houses just as he feeds his retainers at his own, and the subsistence of both comes from his bounty and depends on his pleasure (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). When the landowners spend on tradesmen and artificers instead, the landowners taken together may maintain as many people as before, or more, because rustic hospitality was wasteful. Each landowner, taken singly, contributes only a very small share to the maintenance of any one of them. A tradesman draws his subsistence from a hundred or a thousand different customers. He is therefore in some measure obliged to them all but is not absolutely dependent on any one (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Smith also notes that the older kind of spending meant sharing the produce of the land with tenants and retainers. Foreign commerce and manufactures gave the landowners something they could consume themselves without sharing it with others (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book III, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Kant does not argue this. The passages say the opposite: scepticism does not give definitive answers to the problems of reason.

1. Scepticism offers no solution. Kant says the sceptical procedure "does not present any solution of the problems of reason". It is instead an exercise that awakens reason's circumspection (caution) and points to how reason may establish its legitimate claims (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)).

2. Scepticism gives no certain information about the bounds of knowledge. Its polemic is aimed at the dogmatist, who builds a system without examining its foundations. Taken by itself, it cannot settle the dispute about the rights and powers of human reason (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 31 (edition-specific)).

3. Scepticism is a stage, not the destination. Kant describes dogmatism as the first step and scepticism as the second. A third step, criticism, examines reason itself and fixes its necessary limits. Scepticism is only "a resting place for reason", not its permanent dwelling-place (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 28 (edition-specific)).

4. A sceptic's own doubts are undermined. Kant says the sceptical thinker he discusses "merely declared the understanding to be limited" without showing what its limits were. That thinker's objections rested on contingent facts rather than principles, so his own declarations came to be doubted (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)).

5. Reason itself must answer its own questions. Kant says we may not decline to solve them, because reason is the creator of these ideas. It is therefore bound either to establish their validity or to expose their illusory nature (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). The passages credit scepticism only with preparing the way for this critical work.

top_retrieved.locator: Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 27 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Hume holds that surprising results in the body do not show that nature's laws have failed. When the usual symptoms of health or sickness disappoint our expectation, or medicines do not work with their wonted (usual) powers, the philosopher and physician are not surprised. Nor are they tempted to deny "the necessity and uniformity" of the principles governing the animal economy (the body's workings) (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). His explanation is that the body is a "mighty complicated machine" in which many secret powers lurk, beyond our comprehension. It therefore often appears very uncertain to us. The irregular events that show themselves outwardly are thus no proof that the laws of nature are not observed with the greatest regularity in its internal operations (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §67, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). The irregularity lies in our limited knowledge, not in the laws themselves.

This fits Hume's wider point that, where an effect depends on an intricate machinery or secret structure of parts, we readily attribute our knowledge of it to experience alone. His example is the question of why milk or bread nourishes a man but not a lion or tiger (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Part I, §24, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Hume then applies the same reasoning to human actions: seemingly irregular choices can be explained by someone who knows every circumstance, and the internal principles may operate uniformly despite apparent irregularities (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section VIII, Part I, §68, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Hobbes traces wax candles in Christian ceremonies to pagan processions. In his account, bearing burning torches and candles before the images of the gods belonged to the processions of both the Greeks and the Romans (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Wax Candles, And Torches Lighted, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). The same honor was later given to Roman Emperors. He cites Caligula, who was received amid burning torches, and Caracalla, who was received into Alexandria with incense, flowers, and "Dadouchiais", meaning torches (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Wax Candles, And Torches Lighted, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). Over time, he says, devout but ignorant people often honored their Bishops with the same pomp of wax candles. They also honored the images of our Saviour and the Saints in the Church itself. This is how the use of wax candles came in, and some ancient Councils also established it (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Wax Candles, And Torches Lighted, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)).

This fits his wider claim that Roman Church ceremonies were left over from the conversion of the Gentiles. He calls them "old empty Bottles of Gentilisme" that the Church's Doctors refilled with Christianity (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Wax Candles, And Torches Lighted, paragraph 38 (edition-specific)). He also says that the religious worship now in use was left in the Church by not destroying the images when the Gentiles were converted (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Painting Of Fancies No Idolatry: Abusing Them To Religious Worship Is, paragraph 32 (edition-specific)). The passages do not say specifically when candles were first adopted, and the only dating they give is the vague "in processe of time". Nor do they name the Councils that established the practice.

detail.answer:
Locke divides power into two kinds according to whether a thing can make a change or receive one. He says power is "two-fold": being "able to make, or able to receive any change." The first he calls active power and the second passive power (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He leaves open whether matter has any active power at all. He also leaves open whether created spirits alone can have both kinds. He declines to pursue either question there, since his business is how we come by the idea of power (same passage). He adds that active powers may not be as truly active as our hasty thoughts suppose, and he points us to God and spirits for the clearest idea of active power (same passage).

Locke says sensible things give us plenty of ideas of passive power, because their qualities are in continual flux. Active power, which he calls the more proper meaning of "power," is also instanced everywhere, because whenever we see a change we infer a power able to make it and a possibility in the thing to receive it (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Yet he holds that bodies give us no clear idea of active power. A body that is moving because it was struck is, in his words, undergoing "a passion" rather than an action. A billiard ball only transfers motion and does not produce it. Our clearest idea of active power comes instead from reflecting on the operations of our own minds (same passage).

The same contrast appears in his vocabulary of cause and effect. The efficacy of a power is called "action" in the subject that exerts it. In the subject in which an idea is changed or produced, it is called "passion" (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 22, §11, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: Why does Mill claim that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated?
detail.premise: Mill claims that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated.
detail.answer:
Mill does not claim this. He rejects it. He treats the objection that, when our sentiment of justice is outraged, we think only of the individual case and not of society or any collective interest, and he says it is "no objection against this doctrine" (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). His reasons are as follows.

1. He grants that it is common to feel resentment merely because we have suffered pain, though he calls this "the reverse of commendable" (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). So some people do think only of their own pain. That is not what makes the feeling a moral one.

2. A person whose resentment is "really a moral feeling" first considers whether the act is blameable. Even without saying so to himself, he feels he is asserting a rule that benefits others as well as himself (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). If he regards the act solely as it affects him individually, he is "not consciously just" (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

3. Mill explains the underlying structure. The desire to punish is a natural feeling of retaliation or vengeance. In itself it "has nothing moral in it"; it becomes moral only when subordinated to the social sympathies. A just person resents a hurt to society, and does not resent a hurt to himself unless it is of a kind society has a common interest in repressing (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). He sums up the sentiment as an animal desire to repel a hurt to oneself or to those one sympathizes with, widened to include all persons by enlarged sympathy and intelligent self-interest. From the latter elements it gets its morality, and from the former its energy of self-assertion (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)).

4. He adds that even anti-utilitarians such as Kant implicitly admit this. Kant's principle only has meaning if the interest of mankind collectively is in the agent's mind (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

So the premise of the question is mistaken. In the passages provided, Mill says self-focused resentment is common but not properly moral, and that the sense of justice in its moral form involves concern for others' interests too.

detail.question: What does Kant say about our possession of a priori synthetic knowledge and reason’s responsibility for its own ideas?

expected.author: Immanuel Kant
expected.locator: Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)

top_retrieved.author: Immanuel Kant
top_retrieved.locator: Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)

top_retrieved.author: Immanuel Kant
top_retrieved.locator: Transcendental Dialectic, Book II, Chapter 3, Section VII, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)

top_retrieved.author: Immanuel Kant
top_retrieved.locator: Transcendental Analytic, Book I, Chapter 2, §23, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Kant says we do actually possess à priori synthetical cognitions (knowledge that is independent of experience and adds to our concepts). He takes the principles of the understanding, which anticipate experience, as proof of this (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section II, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). Someone who cannot comprehend how these principles are possible may doubt that they are really à priori. He cannot, however, declare them impossible or call the steps reason has taken under their guidance null (same passage). Doubt about dogmatical philosophy, which proceeds without criticism, is well grounded. But we cannot deny that reason can build a sound philosophy once a thorough critical investigation has prepared the way (same passage).

On reason's responsibility, Kant says that the conceptions and questions of pure reason lie in the sphere of reason itself, not of experience. Reason must therefore settle them and show them to be either valid or inadmissible. We may not decline to do so by appealing to the nature of things or to the limits of human faculties. Reason is the sole creator of these ideas, so it is bound either to establish their validity or to expose their illusory nature (same passage).

detail.answer: Hume judges Cartesian universal doubt to be ineffective as a route to certainty. He describes it as a kind of scepticism that comes before all study and philosophy, and says Descartes and others recommend it as a "sovereign preservative against error and precipitate judgement." It calls for doubting all our former opinions and principles, and even our faculties. We would then have to assure ourselves of those faculties by a chain of reasoning from some original principle that could not be fallacious (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hume gives two objections. First, no such original principle has a prerogative (a special privilege) over other self-evident and convincing principles. Second, even if there were one, we could not advance a step beyond it except by using the very faculties we were supposed to distrust (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). His conclusion is that this doubt, if any human could actually reach it (he says plainly none can), would be entirely incurable. No reasoning could then bring us to assurance and conviction on any subject (Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part I, §116, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). The passages do not say whether Hume thinks any other form of doubt would be more useful. The other Hume passage provided, on mitigated scepticism, does not discuss Cartesian doubt, so I have not used it here.

detail.question: How does Hobbes distinguish between justice in people and justice in actions?

expected.author: Thomas Hobbes
expected.locator: Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)

top_retrieved.author: Thomas Hobbes
top_retrieved.locator: Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Hobbes says the words "Just" and "Unjust" mean one thing when applied to men and another when applied to actions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Applied to men, they signify conformity or inconformity of manners to reason. Applied to actions, they signify conformity or inconformity to reason not of one's manner of life but of particular actions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

A just man is one who takes all the care he can that his actions may all be just, and an unjust man is one who neglects this. Such men are more often called Righteous and Unrighteous, though the meaning is the same (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). One consequence is that a righteous man does not lose that title through one or a few unjust actions that come from sudden passion or a mistake about things or persons. Likewise an unrighteous man does not lose his character for actions he does, or refrains from doing, out of fear, because his will is shaped not by justice but by the apparent benefit of what he is to do (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

Hobbes adds that what gives human actions the "relish of Justice" is a rare nobleness or gallantness of courage, by which a man scorns to depend on fraud or breach of promise for the contentment of his life. This justice of manners is what is meant when justice is called a virtue and injustice a vice (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Burke suggests his countrymen should hold up the British Constitution as an example to the French, rather than take French models for improving their own. He calls it "an invaluable treasure" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 417 (edition-specific)). He credits England's happy situation to the whole Constitution, not to any one part. Much of it comes from what was left standing in earlier reviews and reformations, not only from what was altered or added (same passage). The English should therefore spend their patriotic spirit guarding what they possess from violation. Burke does not rule out alteration, but says that when he changed something, it should be to preserve. He would be led to a remedy by a great grievance, would follow his ancestors, and would repair "as nearly as possible in the style of the building." He urges imitating the caution of their forefathers, who acted from a sense of human ignorance and fallibility. Burke says: "Let us add, if we please, but let us preserve what they have left." The English should stand on the British Constitution and be content to admire, rather than follow, the "aëronauts of France" (same passage). He also wants his countrymen to attend to the true principles of their own domestic laws and keep cherishing them. They should not be taken in by counterfeit wares of "improved liberty" that are dressed up as British products and re-exported from Paris (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). His concern is a spirit of change and a contempt for ancient institutions, and he dislikes revolutions (same passage). The passages do not give a fuller list of specific measures.

Burke says the British people should take it seriously, as "a domestic interest of some moment," to examine "the solidity of the only principle" on which the preacher and his friends acknowledge the king of Great Britain's claim to allegiance (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). His specific worries are these:

- Burke sees a policy behind it. The abstract principle that popular choice is necessary for lawful sovereignty is introduced while it seems not to threaten the king. Congregations grow used to it as if it were undisputed, and it is stored up "for future use." Government is soothed with a favor it has no claim to, while the security it shares with all governments, so far as opinion is security, is taken away (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

He holds that the king reigns by a fixed rule of succession under the laws of his country (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 23 (edition-specific)).
- Whatever evasions are tried, the declared principle of a right in the people to choose remains maintained (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 24 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: How does Mill distinguish between types of government interference in trade?
detail.answer:
Mill separates kinds of interference with trade by asking whether the principle of individual liberty is actually at stake.

1. Interference that restricts producers and sellers is mainly not a liberty question. Mill says trade is a social act, so it falls within society's jurisdiction. Restrictions on trade are restraints, and restraint as such is an evil. But they concern conduct that society is competent to restrain, and they are wrong only because they fail to produce the results they aim at. The doctrine of Free Trade therefore rests on grounds different from the principle of individual liberty (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

2. Many questions about the limits of that doctrine are likewise not liberty questions. Examples are public control to prevent fraud by adulteration, sanitary precautions, and protections for workers in dangerous occupations. Liberty enters only because leaving people alone is generally better than controlling them, all else equal. Mill says such control is in principle undeniably legitimate (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

3. Other trade interferences are essentially questions of liberty. These are cases where the object is to make a commodity impossible or difficult to obtain, such as the Maine Law, the prohibition of opium imports into China, and restrictions on the sale of poisons. Mill says these are objectionable as infringements not on the liberty of the producer or seller but on that of the buyer (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

Mill also sets aside a further class of cases that do not turn on liberty. There the question is not about restraining individuals but about helping them, that is, whether government should do something for their benefit (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). He says objections to interference that does not infringe liberty may be of three kinds (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 17 (edition-specific)). The first is that the thing is likely to be better done by individuals than by government, which condemns government interference with the ordinary processes of industry (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)). The passages provided do not state the other two kinds.

detail.answer: Kant says that if general logic is used as an organon (a tool for actually producing knowledge), it is grossly misapplied. General logic is only a canon of judgement. It gives cognitions the form of the understanding, but the form alone cannot supply material (objective) truth. It abstracts from all content and from the relation of cognition to its object, and it considers only the form of thought (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Logic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Real, substantive knowledge is to be sought only in the objective sciences, and logic is merely a propædeutic (a preparatory discipline) (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Preface to the Second Edition, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). detail.answer:
The question's premise does not match the passages. Burke does not argue that the paper currency scheme will distribute power equally among citizens. He argues the opposite: the scheme will concentrate power in a few hands. He says its one certain effect is "producing an oligarchy in every one of the republics" (an oligarchy is rule by a small group). Because the paper circulation is not backed by real money deposited, and is forced in place of the kingdom's coin, it becomes the substance of the revenue and the medium of all commercial and civil intercourse. Burke concludes that whatever power, authority and influence remain must pass into the hands of "the managers and conductors of this circulation" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 331 (edition-specific)).

The closest Burke comes to 'equality' is a different point. He says the Assembly wanted to "put every individual on the same bottom" and bind the nation in one guilty interest, forcing even the reluctant to share in the pillage of Church property by making the paper circulation compulsory (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 220 (edition-specific)). This describes a political device for securing the Assembly's power, not an equal distribution of power. Burke also calls the compulsory paper currency a violent outrage upon credit, property and liberty (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 221 (edition-specific)).

The Adam Smith passages supplied discuss the risks of paper money generally, but they say nothing about Burke's claim or about equal power.

detail.question: According to Mill, should society always punish individuals for personal failings such as imprudence or lack of dignity?
detail.premise: Mill believes society should punish individuals for personal failings even when these do not harm others.
detail.answer:
No. Mill argues that society should not punish people for purely self-regarding failings such as imprudence or lack of personal dignity, though he allows some qualifications.

He distinguishes the "loss of consideration" a person may rightly incur through defects of prudence or personal dignity from the reprobation due to an offence against others' rights (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). For merely self-regarding faults, we may express distaste and stand aloof. We do not feel called on to make the person's life uncomfortable, because he already bears the whole penalty of his error. Rather than punish him, we should try to alleviate his punishment by showing him how to avoid the evils his conduct brings (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). Punishment with the express purpose of inflicting pain is reserved for those who infringe rules protecting others (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

The same principle appears in his two maxims. The individual is not accountable to society for actions that concern only himself. Society may respond only with advice, instruction, persuasion, and avoidance. Accountability and social or legal punishment apply to actions prejudicial to others (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

Mill considers and rejects the objection that society should protect mature persons from their own vices, as it protects children. He holds that the inconvenience of such conduct is one society can afford to bear for the sake of human freedom (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). He says society had the whole period of childhood in which to train its members, so it has itself to blame if they grow up incapable of rational conduct (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). He also says that coercing people into prudence or temperance tends to provoke rebellion (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). The objection itself is set out in Chapter 4, paragraph 9, which asks whether law and opinion should repress vices such as gambling, drunkenness, or idleness (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)).

There are qualifications. When self-regarding conduct leads a person to violate a distinct obligation to others, such as failing to pay debts or support a family, he may be justly punished. But the punishment is for the breach of duty, not for the extravagance (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Mill also says drunkenness is ordinarily not a fit subject for legislative interference, but a person convicted of violence while drunk may be placed under a special restriction. Idleness cannot without tyranny be legally punished, except in particular cases such as breach of contract or receiving public support (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Smith describes a fall in the value of gold and silver, which he ties to the discovery of more abundant American mines. He also separates the metals' value in each other from their value in labour or goods.

**Relative value (gold against silver).** Before the discovery, an ounce of fine gold was worth about 10 to 12 ounces of fine silver in the European mines. About the middle of the last century (Smith's "last century" is the 1600s), the ratio was between 1 to 14 and 1 to 15. Gold therefore rose in nominal value, meaning the quantity of silver given for it (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 91 (edition-specific)).

**Real value.** In the same passage, Smith says both metals sank in real value, meaning the quantity of labour they could purchase, but silver sank more than gold. He says it seems the American silver mines were proportionally even more fertile than the gold ones (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 91 (edition-specific)).

**The general mechanism.** More abundant mines bring more of the metals to market, while the goods they must be exchanged for stay the same. Equal quantities of the metals must then be exchanged for smaller quantities of commodities, so the metals lose value (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 40 (edition-specific)). He says the discovery diminished the value of gold and silver in Europe (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 5, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

**Silver against corn.** Smith says the American mines seem to have been the sole cause of silver's fall in value relative to corn. Supply grew faster than demand, so the metal's value sank considerably (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 50 (edition-specific)). He adds that the discovery seems to have had no very sensible effect on English prices until after 1570 (same passage).

**Timing.** Between 1630 and 1640, or about 1636, the effect of the discovery on silver's value appears to have been completed. Silver seems never to have sunk lower relative to corn than at that time, and it seems to have risen somewhat since (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 53 (edition-specific)).

**Cause of the decline.** Smith says the value of gold and silver gradually diminished as Europe grew wealthier. He attributes this to the accidental discovery of more abundant mines, not to any increase in Europe's real wealth (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 11, Part III, paragraph 144 (edition-specific)).

**Smith's caution.** He hedges the claim that the decline is still continuing. Of the view that the diminution is still going on gradually, he says it is "commonly supposed" but that he apprehends it is held "without any certain proof" (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 5, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)). Elsewhere he says it is supposed, perhaps "without much foundation," that the metals have been steadily sinking in value because of continual imports from the Spanish West Indies (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book IV, Chapter 1, paragraph 14 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Wollstonecraft describes a sequence in which power first rests with chiefs and priests, then hardens into monarchy and hierarchy, and is later softened into covert corruption. In the infancy of society, as people were emerging from barbarism, chiefs and priests worked on "hope and fear," which she calls the most powerful springs of savage conduct, and so "must have had unbounded sway" (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). She says an aristocracy is "naturally the first form of government." Clashing interests then lose their balance ("equipoise"). A monarchy and a hierarchy break out of the confusion of ambitious struggles, and feudal tenures secure the foundation of both (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). She presents this as what "appears to be" the origin of monarchial and priestly power and the dawn of civilization, so the account is stated with some tentativeness (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). She then says this does not stay stable. Through foreign wars and internal insurrections the people gain some power, which obliges rulers to cover their oppression with a show of right. As wars, agriculture, commerce and literature expand the mind, despots must use covert corruption to hold the power once taken by open force. Luxury and superstition spread this corruption, and the court figure becomes a luxurious sensualist who turns the contagion into an instrument of tyranny (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 1, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What does Locke argue about the relationship between conquest and the establishment of government?
detail.answer:
Locke argues that conquest is not a true origin of government. Governments originally rise only from the consent of the people, but the noise of war has led many to mistake the force of arms for that consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He compares conquest to demolishing a house: it is no nearer to building a new one. Conquest may often make way for a new frame of commonwealth by destroying the old one, but without the people's consent it can never erect a new one (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

Earlier, Locke says history shows that the peaceful beginnings of government were laid in consent. He adds the word 'peaceful' because he means to treat conquest, which some esteem a way of beginning governments, separately (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 8, §112, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). He also says that governments begun in peace were founded on men's natural freedom and made by the people's consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 8, §104, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)).

Locke also limits what conquest can give a conqueror. He gets no power over those who conquered alongside him. Using the Norman conquest as his example, he says the Normans who helped William, and their descendants, are freemen and not subjects by conquest (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §177, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Over the vanquished, he says the conqueror's claim gives only the title that bare force gives to the stronger over the weaker. If that were enough, whoever is strongest would have a right to whatever he pleases to seize (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §184, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Even if a conqueror in a just war did have a right to the conquered's estates (which Locke says he plainly does not), absolute power would not follow for the continuing government. The descendants of the conquered are freemen, and whatever property is granted to them cannot be taken from them without their own consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §193, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: According to Hume, what distinguishes belief from mere imagination or fiction?

top_retrieved.author: Immanuel Kant
top_retrieved.locator: Doctrine of Method, Chapter 1, Section III, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)

detail.answer: For Hume, belief differs from imagination or fiction in how an idea is felt, not in what the idea contains. The imagination can mix and join ideas freely and can picture invented events with every circumstance of time and place (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Yet we cannot simply choose to believe: we can join a man's head to a horse's body, but we cannot believe such an animal ever existed (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). A single special idea attached to some conceptions cannot be the difference, because the mind could then add it to any fiction at will (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Hume concludes that the difference lies in a sentiment or feeling attached to belief and not to fiction. This feeling does not depend on the will and cannot be commanded at pleasure (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). It arises from nature. When an object is presented to memory or the senses, custom carries the imagination to conceive the object usually conjoined with it, and this conception is attended by a feeling different from the loose reveries of the fancy (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §39, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He describes this feeling as a more vivid, lively, forcible, firm, steady conception of an object than imagination alone can reach. He adds that belief lies in the manner of conception and its feeling to the mind, not in the nature or order of the ideas (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Hume admits that this feeling is very hard, perhaps impossible, to define perfectly, and that philosophy can only say belief is something felt by the mind that distinguishes the ideas of the judgement from the fictions of the imagination (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He summarizes the doctrine as a sentiment of belief that is a conception more intense and steady than what attends mere fictions. This manner of conception arises from a customary conjunction of the object with something present to memory or the senses (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section V, Part II, §40, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He offers this as a supposition ("let us ... allow") that he expects to generalize, not as a final proof.

detail.answer:
Smith says wages of labour vary more from place to place than the price of provisions does. Bread and butchers' meat cost about the same through most of the united kingdom, and most retail goods are as cheap or cheaper in great towns than in remote parts. Wages in a great town and its neighbourhood are often a fourth or fifth (twenty or twenty-five per cent) higher than a few miles away (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). His examples: eighteen pence a day in London and its neighbourhood, falling to fourteen or fifteen pence a few miles off; ten pence in Edinburgh, falling to eightpence a few miles away (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)). He argues that if goods were this unevenly priced they would be transported until prices levelled, but man is 'of all sorts of luggage, the most difficult to be transported.' He concludes that if the labouring poor can support families where wages are lowest, they must be in affluence where wages are highest (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 29 (edition-specific)).

He adds that variations in the price of labour do not correspond, in place or time, with those in the price of provisions, and are frequently quite opposite (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, Chapter 8, paragraph 30 (edition-specific)). detail.answer:
Burke holds that the French ministers occupy a degrading and perilous post, for several reasons drawn from his own words.

1. The office has lost its dignity. He says that in all other countries the office of ministers of state is of the highest dignity, but in France it is "full of peril, and incapable of glory" (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)). He adds that they can gain no fame from it.

2. They are exposed to attack but cannot defend themselves. Rivals, empowered by the Constitution, can attack them in their vital parts. The ministers can answer only in the "degrading character of culprits" (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)). He also notes that they are the only people in France incapable of a share in the national councils (same passage).

3. Responsibility without power. Burke says responsibility may prevent crimes, but it cannot supply "active and zealous service" (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

4. They are caught between two masters. They lack confidence from the sovereign on whom they were forced, and from the Assembly that forced them upon him. The functions of their office are carried out by committees of the Assembly, regardless of the ministers' authority. Burke sums this up: they "execute, without power," are "responsible, without discretion," and "deliberate, without choice." Serving under "two sovereigns," with influence over neither, they must sometimes betray one, sometimes the other, and always themselves (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

5. They see the damage done. Burke says they stand on an "eminence of humiliation" and must feel their country's degraded situation and their own "utter incapacity of serving it." He is astonished they have not resigned and would not have stood in their situation (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)). Burke assumes, but does not assert as certain, that they wished the Revolution well.

Locke says that a person who thinks for himself and pursues truth gets real satisfaction from the effort, whatever the result. detail.answer:
Smith says the way France collects its taxes strongly affects how much of what the people pay actually reaches the crown. He names eight main sources of French royal revenue: the taille, the capitation, the two vingtiemes, the gabelles, the aides, the traites, the domaine, and the farm of tobacco (a "farm" means collection is contracted out). The last five are, in most provinces, under farm. The first three are levied by an administration under the direct inspection and direction of government. It is "universally acknowledged" that, in proportion to what they take from the people, the directly administered taxes bring more into the prince's treasury than the farmed ones, whose administration is "much more wasteful and expensive" (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 205 (edition-specific)).

Smith also proposes reforms aimed at efficiency. Replacing the taille and capitation with more vingtiemes could preserve the crown's revenue and greatly reduce collection costs (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 206 (edition-specific)). Making the gabelle, aides, traites, tobacco taxes, customs and excises uniform across the kingdom would let them be levied at much less expense (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 206 (edition-specific)). His third reform, to put all these taxes under an administration under the government's immediate direction, is cut off in the passage, so I cannot say how he completes it.

Smith adds that the French crown's receipts fall far short of what might be expected. In 1765 and 1766 the revenue paid into the treasury was under fifteen million pounds sterling, less than half of what a Britain-style contribution would give, even though the French people are generally acknowledged to be more oppressed by taxes (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 2, Part II, paragraph 207 (edition-specific)). The passages do not explicitly attribute this shortfall to collection methods alone.

detail.answer:
The question's premise does not match the passages. In these passages Locke does not say private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies. He argues the opposite: that property can arise legitimately, and that it arose through labour. The passages do not mention a view that property is never justified.

Locke starts from the claim that God gave the earth to mankind in common. He then sets out to show how men might come to have a property in parts of it without any express compact of all the commoners (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §25, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

His answer is labour. A man is master of himself and proprietor of his own person and its labour, so he has in himself the great foundation of property. Even though the things of nature are given in common, what he applies to his support is his own (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §44, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)). For example, the deer belongs to the Indian who killed it, though it was previously common to everyone. Whoever bestows labour on something thereby makes it his goods (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §30, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). Locke says that in the beginning labour gave a right of property wherever someone employed it on what was common. Later, communities settled the boundaries of property by laws and agreement (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §45, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)).

Locke also argues that early appropriation was not unjust. The measure of property was set by the extent of a man's labour and the conveniences of life, so no one could take so much as to injure a neighbour. Others still had room for as good and as large a possession (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §36, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Locke also treats property as something government must protect. He says the enjoyment of property in the state of nature is very unsafe, which is why men join society for the mutual preservation of their lives, liberties and estates, which he calls by the general name property (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 9, §123, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He adds that the supreme power cannot take any part of a man's property without his own consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 11, §138, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Locke says he is willing to change his opinions on liberty when he finds reason to, though he is not moved by every objection.

1. He describes himself as "a lover of truth, and not a worshipper of my own doctrines." He admits that he changed his opinion from what he gave in an earlier edition, and says he thinks he found grounds for the change (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §74, paragraph 78). He says he was neither "so vain as to fancy infallibility" nor so disingenuous as to hide his mistakes for fear of harming his reputation. He was therefore not ashamed to publish what a "severer inquiry" suggested (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §74, paragraph 78).

2. In the Epistle to the Reader he says he found reason "somewhat to alter" his earlier thoughts about what gives the last determination to the Will in voluntary actions. He acknowledges this as freely as he first published his earlier view. He says he is more concerned to renounce an opinion of his own than to oppose another's when truth appears against it (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 10).

3. He also says what prompted the revision. He himself feared the chapter contained a mistake, and a judicious friend suspected one. A stricter review turned up a "very easy and scarce observable slip," in which he had put one seemingly indifferent word for another (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §73, paragraph 77).

4. His willingness has limits. He says he will give up an opinion on the first evidence of error. But he has not received light from the printed objections against his book, and nothing urged against it has led him to change his sense of the questioned points. He suggests that readers may be inattentive or that his expressions may be obscure, so that he is often misunderstood (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 10).

5. He does not expect everyone to agree with the revision. Some may prefer his former notions, some the later ones, and some neither. He would be beholden to anyone who could fairly clear the subject of the remaining difficulties (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §74, paragraph 78).

detail.answer:
Kant describes reason, in its logical use, as the faculty of conclusion, or "mediate judgement" (a judgement reached by way of another). It works by subsuming (placing under) the condition of a possible judgement under the condition of a given judgement (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

The process has three steps, which make up a syllogism:
1. The given judgement is the general rule, the major. The understanding thinks it (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).
2. The minor subsumes a cognition under the condition of the rule. Kant says this is done by means of the judgement (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).
3. The conclusion determines the cognition through the predicate of the rule, which Kant says is determining it à priori by means of reason (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Because the rule asserts something generally under a condition, and that condition is met in a particular case, what holds in general must also hold in that case (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Kant's example runs from "All compound is changeable", to "Bodies are compound", to "Consequently, bodies are changeable". Reason thus reaches a cognition through a series of conditions (premisses) (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Book I, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

When the conclusion is a judgement about a quite different object, I look in the understanding for a general rule under whose condition the assertion stands. If the object can be subsumed under that condition, the conclusion follows from a rule valid for other objects too (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

The process can be extended. The rule can itself be treated as a conclusion, and its condition sought through a prosyllogism, a syllogism leading up to the premiss. Kant takes the peculiar principle of reason in its logical use to be finding the unconditioned for the conditioned cognition of the understanding, which completes its unity (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). Reason thereby tries to bring the variety of the understanding's cognitions under the smallest possible number of principles, producing the highest unity (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Introduction, Section II, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Kant also distinguishes two employments of reason in deducing the particular from the general. If the general is certain and given, the particular is necessarily determined by subsumption; this is the demonstrative or apodeictic employment. If the general is only problematical, a mere idea, the particular cases are examined, and if all of them follow from the rule, its universality is inferred; this is the hypothetical employment (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

Kant says the object associated with the idea of systematic unity is a mere idea, not something assumed to be real in itself. Reason cannot think systematic unity without also thinking an object of the idea. That object cannot be presented in any experience and contains no concrete example of complete systematic unity. He calls it an ens rationis ratiocinatae, a being of reasoning, and says it is "a mere idea and is not assumed to be a thing which is real absolutely and in itself" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 46 (edition-specific)). It serves only as the "problematical foundation" of the connection the mind introduces among phenomena. We look at that connection as if it came from the supposed being corresponding to the idea, but all we aim at is a secure foundation for the systematic unity of experience (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 46 (edition-specific)).

This fits his wider account of the status of systematic unity. As a mere idea it is a projected unity, "not to be regarded as given, but only in the light of a problem" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 8 (edition-specific)). It is a subjective maxim, not an objective principle extending over objects. It is also not a constitutive principle that determines an object, but a regulative one (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)). Kant also warns against hypostatizing the principle, meaning treating it as a real thing, and against giving a Supreme Intelligence an anthropomorphic (human-like) determination. He calls this perverted reason, and says it loses the unity of nature (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 54 (edition-specific)).

The passages also contain some qualifications. Kant says the principle is objective "although only in an indefinite respect" (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 45 (edition-specific)). He also says we must suppose the idea of the systematic unity of nature to possess objective validity and necessity in relation to the criterion of empirical truth (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)). Elsewhere, he says it is natural to assume a legislative reason corresponding to the idea of unity (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Transcendental Dialectic, Appendix, paragraph 56 (edition-specific)). These remarks concern the idea's validity and the naturalness of the assumption. They do not say the corresponding object is real in itself.

detail.answer:
Hobbes says the word 'Church' (Greek Ecclesia) signifies "divers things" in the Books of Holy Scripture (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The meanings he lists are:

1. A house. Sometimes, though not often, it means God's House, that is, a Temple where Christians assemble for public holy duties. Hobbes calls this a metaphorical use, since the word really names the congregation assembled there. It was later used for the building itself (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. An assembly. When not taken for a house, it means what Ecclesia meant in the Grecian Common-wealths: a congregation or assembly of citizens called forth to hear the Magistrate speak. If called by lawful authority it was a lawful Church (Ecclesia Legitima). If stirred up by tumultuous and seditious clamor it was a confused Church (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

3. Other scriptural senses. It is sometimes taken for the men who have a right to be of the Congregation though not actually assembled, meaning the whole multitude of Christian men however dispersed. In this sense Christ is said to be Head of the Church. It can also mean a certain part of Christians, or the Elect only (the Church Triumphant, or Church To Come). It can also mean a congregation assembled of professors of Christianity, whether their profession is true or counterfeit (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

4. Hobbes's own definition. He says the Church can be taken as one Person only in the sense of a lawfully assembled congregation. In that sense he defines a CHURCH as a company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign, at whose command they ought to assemble and without whose authority they ought not (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, In What Sense The Church Is One Person Church Defined, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not support the premise. Hobbes argues the opposite: that the sovereign should regulate opinions and doctrines.

Hobbes says it belongs to the sovereign to judge which opinions and doctrines are averse to peace and which conduce to it, and to decide who examines books before they are published (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). His reason is that men's actions proceed from their opinions, so governing opinions well is how their actions are governed toward peace and concord (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). He concludes that the sovereign should be judge, or appoint all judges, of opinions and doctrines, as something necessary to peace and to prevent discord and civil war (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)).

A related passage points the same way. Hobbes treats the doctrine that acting against one's conscience is always sin as repugnant to civil society. In a commonwealth, he says, the law is the public conscience. If private consciences, which he calls private opinions, were followed instead, the commonwealth would be distracted (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 29, Erroneous Conscience, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

The view that authorities should not control opinion appears in John Stuart Mill, not Hobbes. Mill calls the power to coerce opinion illegitimate (John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The passages give no Hobbesian argument against sovereign regulation of doctrines.
