detail.answer:
The question reverses Hume's claim. He says the opposite of any matter of fact is possible, because it can be conceived without contradiction. His reasoning runs as follows.

1. Matters of fact are not established the way demonstrable truths are. The contrary of every matter of fact is still possible, because it never implies a contradiction. The mind conceives it as easily and distinctly as the truth (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Part I, §21, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. His example is that the sun will not rise tomorrow. This is no less intelligible than the claim that it will rise, and it implies no more contradiction. So we cannot demonstrate its falsehood, because a demonstratively false proposition would imply a contradiction and could not be distinctly conceived (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section IV, Part I, §21, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

3. In the later passage, he says enquiries into matter of fact and existence cannot be demonstrated, and that no negation of a fact can involve a contradiction. The non-existence of any being is as clear and distinct an idea as its existence. A proposition denying a being may be false, but it is just as conceivable and intelligible as one affirming it (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part III, §132, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

4. He contrasts this with the sciences properly so called. There, a false proposition is confused and unintelligible. His example is that the cube root of 64 equals half of 10, which cannot be distinctly conceived. By contrast, the claim that Caesar or the angel Gabriel never existed may be false, but it is perfectly conceivable and implies no contradiction (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section XII, Part III, §132, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

The Kant passages supplied do not address Hume's claim, so I have not used them.

detail.question: What does Hume suggest about the origins of widely believed extraordinary stories?
detail.answer:
Hume does not treat widely believed extraordinary stories as evidence that something supernatural happened. He traces them to ordinary human tendencies.

1. Hume says that forged miracles, prophecies and supernatural events, which have been detected or have exposed themselves by their absurdity in every age, show a strong human propensity (natural inclination) toward the extraordinary and marvellous. He argues this should make us suspicious of all such reports (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). He compares this to how marriage rumours spread: the pleasure of telling and being first to report interesting news spreads them. He asks whether the same passions, and stronger ones, lead people to report religious miracles with great vehemence (same passage).

2. Surprise and wonder are an agreeable emotion that inclines us to believe the events that produce them. Even people who cannot believe a miracle enjoy it second-hand and take pride in exciting others' admiration (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

3. When religion joins the love of wonder, Hume says, common sense ends. The religious narrator may be an enthusiast (someone carried away by religious fervour) who imagines what is unreal, may knowingly persist in a falsehood for a holy cause, or may be driven by vanity and self-interest. His hearers often lack the judgement to examine his evidence, or give it up on principle, and passion and a heated imagination disturb their reasoning. Hume sums up: "Their credulity increases his impudence" (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §93, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

4. Such tales abound among ignorant and barbarous nations. Civilized peoples receive them from ignorant ancestors who handed them down with the authority that attends received opinions. Hume says the marvels thin out as we approach enlightened ages, because they come from the usual human propensity toward the marvellous. That inclination may be checked by sense and learning but can never be thoroughly extirpated (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §94, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

5. Hume says it is nothing strange that men lie in all ages. He asserts that the renowned lies that grew to a monstrous height began like the marvellous tales that wise people scorn and the vulgar eventually abandon. They were simply sown in a more suitable soil (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §94, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

6. Many such stories have been exposed early or have sunk into oblivion. So when such reports spread, the obvious explanation lies in the known and natural principles of credulity and delusion, not in a miraculous violation of nature's laws (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section X, Part II, §97, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
For Hobbes, a crime is one kind of sin, not a separate thing. A sin is the wider category: it is not only breaking a law but also any contempt of the legislator, and it can lie in an act, in words, in an omission, or in the intention to transgress (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). A crime is a sin that consists in committing, by deed or word, what the law forbids, or in omitting what it commands. So every crime is a sin, but not every sin is a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

The dividing line is whether another person can accuse. Intending to steal or kill is a sin, because God sees thoughts and can charge a man with them. But an intention that never shows itself by any outward act leaves no place for human accusation (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hobbes backs this with the Greek and Latin words. The Greek word translated 'Sinne' means any swerving from the law, while the words translated 'Crime' mean only the sin one man may accuse another of. The Latin peccatum covers all deviation from the law, whereas crimen covers only sins that can be made to appear before a judge, and so are not mere intentions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

The two also depend on different laws. Sin relates to law in general and crime to the civil law. Where law ceases, sin ceases, but since the law of nature is eternal, violating covenants, ingratitude, arrogance and other acts contrary to moral virtue never cease to be sin. When civil law ceases, crimes cease, because only the law of nature is left. Then there is no place for accusation: each man is his own judge, accused only by his own conscience. If his intention is wrong, his act is a sin but not a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Where No Civill Law Is, There Is No Crime, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Kant's answer is qualified: human reason can recognize that the moral law is necessary, but it cannot make that necessity fully comprehensible.

1. Moral laws carry absolute necessity. In the Groundwork, a law with moral force must "carry with it absolute necessity", so its basis cannot lie in human nature or circumstances but only a priori in pure reason (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Preface, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). In the Critique of Pure Reason he assumes there are pure moral laws that are "absolutely imperative" and therefore necessary in all respects. He says he is warranted in this assumption by enlightened moralists and by the moral judgement of every person (Immanuel Kant, The Critique of Pure Reason, Doctrine of Method, Chapter 2, Section II, paragraph 8 (edition-specific)).

2. Reason can reach the necessity of the idea of freedom. Kant says we can assign the only hypothesis on which a categorical imperative is possible, the idea of freedom, and can "discern the necessity of this hypothesis". He holds this is enough for the practical conviction that the imperative and the moral law are valid. But how this hypothesis itself is possible can never be discerned by any human reason (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 32 (edition-specific)). He also says that explaining how pure reason can be practical, or how it produces a purely moral interest, is beyond human reason (same passage).

3. The unconditional necessity of the law is not comprehended. Reason by its nature pushes toward a consciousness of necessity. Yet it can discern necessity only by supposing a condition, so it keeps seeking the unconditionally necessary without being able to make it comprehensible to itself. Kant therefore says this is an objection to human reason in general, not a fault in his deduction of the supreme principle of morality. He adds that explaining the necessity by some assumed interest would stop the law from being a supreme law of reason. His conclusion is that we do not comprehend the practical unconditional necessity of the moral imperative, yet we comprehend its incomprehensibility, and this is all that can fairly be demanded of philosophy at the limit of human reason (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 35 (edition-specific)).

4. Related limit on explaining moral interest. Kant says it is quite impossible for us to explain how and why the universality of the maxim as a law, that is, morality, interests us. He affirms only that the law does not bind us because it interests us. It interests us because it is valid for us as intelligences, since it has its source in our will (Immanuel Kant, Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals, Third Section, paragraph 31 (edition-specific)).

The passages only partly answer this. They do not discuss a sovereign who expressly commands a subject to break the law. They discuss a nearby case: acts the law condemns but the sovereign tacitly approves by 'other manifest signes of his will'. Hobbes reasons that the lawmaker's will is itself a law, so the case contains two contradictory laws. Hobbes also holds that the sovereign shares the blame, because he attaches punishments to observing his law as well as to breaking it. He is 'in part a cause of the transgression', and so the delinquent should not be rigorously punished (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)). detail.question: According to Locke, why does the bond between male and female animals sometimes last beyond mating?

top_retrieved.author: Mary Wollstonecraft
top_retrieved.work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

detail.answer:
Locke's answer is that the bond lasts only as long as the young need support. He says the purpose of the conjunction between male and female is "not barely procreation, but the continuation of the species." So it ought to last after procreation for as long as is necessary to nourish and support the young, who must be sustained by those who begot them until they can provide for themselves (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He says the inferior creatures steadily obey this rule (same passage).

He gives examples. In grass-eating viviparous animals (those that bear live young), the conjunction lasts no longer than the act of copulation. The dam's teat is enough to nourish the young until they can feed on grass, and the male can contribute nothing to their sustenance (same passage). In beasts of prey the conjunction lasts longer. The dam cannot well support herself and her numerous offspring by her own prey alone, so the male's assistance is necessary until the young can prey for themselves (same passage). Birds are similar. Their young need food in the nest, so the cock and hen stay mates until the young can use their wings and provide for themselves. Locke excepts some domestic birds, where plenty of food excuses the cock (same passage).

For humans, Locke adds that the bond lasts longer because the female commonly conceives again before the earlier child can shift for itself. This obliges the father to stay in conjugal society longer. In other creatures, whose young can subsist before procreation returns, "the conjugal bond dissolves of itself" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §80, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

Smith's passages on forts and garrisons concern the African trade, where the regulated company's committee manages them. They point to several weaknesses in how such forts are overseen and governed.

1. Misaligned incentives in regulated companies. Smith says the directors of a regulated company have no particular interest in the prosperity of the company's general trade, for whose sake the forts are maintained. The decay of that trade may even benefit their own private trade by reducing competitors (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)). Joint-stock company directors, by contrast, have no separable private trade, so they are more likely to give the continual, careful attention that maintenance requires (same passage).

2. Lack of funds. Regulated-company directors manage no common capital. They have only the casual revenue from admission fines and corporation duties, so even with the same interest they can seldom attend to the forts as effectively (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 34 (edition-specific)). Smith therefore concludes that a regulated company is better suited to maintaining a public minister, a business needing scarcely any attention and only a moderate, limited expense.

3. Weak accountability and supervision. Parliament grants about £13,000 a year, and the committee must account annually to the cursitor baron of exchequer. Smith says parliament, which gives so little attention to millions, is unlikely to give much to this sum. He adds that the cursitor baron is unlikely to be skilled in the proper expense of forts and garrisons (Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter 1, Part III, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)).

4. Limited inspection and no authority to correct. Navy captains or other officers appointed by the admiralty may inquire into the forts and report. But the admiralty board seems to have no direct jurisdiction over the committee and no authority to correct it. The captains are also not supposed to be deeply learned in fortification (same passage).

5. Feeble penalties and weak motivation. Apart from direct malversation or embezzlement, the worst punishment a committee-man faces is removal from an office held for three years with very small lawful emoluments. Smith says the fear of this can never force continual, careful attention to a business in which he has no other interest (same passage).

6. Alleged poor performance. The committee is accused of sending bricks and stones from England to repair Cape Coast Castle, despite several extraordinary parliamentary grants. The materials were said to be of such bad quality that the text breaks off there (same passage). Smith presents this as an accusation, and the passage does not show how it ended.

The passages do not describe oversight of British forts and garrisons more generally. They cover only the company-run African forts.

detail.answer:
In the passage that addresses this directly, Hume says there is no real ground for suspecting that the science of the mind (his "mental geography," the study of the mind's powers and faculties) is "uncertain and chimerical" (chimerical means imaginary or illusory). The one exception he allows is a scepticism so extreme that it would undermine all speculation and even action (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

Hume's reasons are as follows. It cannot be doubted that the mind has several distinct powers and faculties. What is distinct in immediate perception can be distinguished by reflexion (reflection). So there is a truth and falsehood in propositions on this subject, and these lie within the compass of human understanding (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He gives obvious distinctions, such as will versus understanding and imagination versus passions. He adds that finer, more philosophical distinctions are "no less real and certain, though more difficult to be comprehended" (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He also points to recent successes in these enquiries as giving a juster notion of the "certainty and solidity" of this branch of learning. He asks whether it is worthwhile to chart the planets while overlooking those who successfully delineate the parts of the mind (David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, Section I, §8, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not say how Hume reconciles this confidence with his scepticism elsewhere. Kant's remarks about Hume concern causality and metaphysics, not the certainty of the science of the mind, so I do not use them here.

detail.answer:
Burke raises several concerns about how the confiscated Church lands are financed and managed. They fall into three groups.

1. The fund carries new charges. The Assembly wanted to show the Church-land fund as a surplus free of all charges. Burke says it has instead been burdened with compensation for the disbanded judiciary and for suppressed offices and estates. He cannot calculate the amount but says it "unquestionably amounts to many French millions" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)). The fund must also pay an annuity of four hundred and eighty thousand pounds sterling as interest on the first assignats (the paper currency issued against the lands), "if they choose to keep faith" (same passage).

2. Management has been left to the municipalities. Burke asks whether the Assembly has ever fairly stated the expense of managing the Church lands. They are in the hands of the municipalities and a "legion of unknown under-agents" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)). He also says the framers of the scheme were bound to make their bank a real fund of credit (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 401 (edition-specific)).

3. The sale terms and the effects of a mass sale are harmful.
- Burke says that putting so much land on the market at once would defeat the profits the confiscation was meant to bring. It would depreciate the value of those lands and of all landed estates in France. It would also divert circulating money from trade to land (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 219 (edition-specific)).
- Burke says the Assembly's actual plan is to sell to the highest bidder but require only part of the price up front, with twelve years allowed for the rest. He describes this as letting in "a body of purchasers without money" and as in effect a gift (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 222 (edition-specific)).
- He predicts that these purchasers will pay out of the rents, the spoil of building materials, waste in woods, and money wrung from the peasantry. He expects extortion, because the estates are held under the uncertain settlement of a new political system (same passage).

The passages do not give a full accounting of the sums involved. Burke himself says he cannot ascertain the amount of one of the charges.

detail.question: What misconception about the meaning of 'utility' does Mill address in this paragraph?
detail.answer:
In Chapter 2, paragraph 1, Mill addresses the mistaken belief that supporters of utility use the word in a narrow, everyday sense in which "utility" is opposed to pleasure. He calls this an "ignorant blunder" (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He says that every writer from Epicurus to Bentham who upheld the theory meant by utility not something distinct from pleasure but "pleasure itself, together with exemption from pain" (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). Instead of setting the useful against the agreeable or the ornamental, they declared that the useful includes these, among other things (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

Mill adds that the public has caught up the word "utilitarian" knowing only its sound, and so uses it to mean the rejection or neglect of pleasure in some forms, such as beauty, ornament or amusement. Sometimes this is meant as disparagement and sometimes as a compliment, as though it implied superiority to frivolity (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He also notes the inconsistency that the same people accuse the theory of reducing everything to pleasure in its grossest form. The theory is thus called "impracticably dry" or "too practicably voluptuous" depending on word order (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke gives several connected reasons for disliking the constant praise of resistance and revolution.

1. It makes an emergency remedy into a daily habit. He says he never liked "this continual talk of resistance and revolution, or the practice of making the extreme medicine of the Constitution its daily bread." He argues that this makes society dangerously sickly ("valetudinary"). He compares it to taking periodic doses of poison and stimulants to our love of liberty. He also fears that anniversary sermons commemorating the Revolution will cheat people of its principles and benefits (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 112 (edition-specific)).

2. It damages moral sentiments for no political gain. In his view, the politics of revolution harden the breast to prepare it for desperate strokes that sometimes occur in extreme cases. Since those occasions may never arrive, the mind picks up a "gratuitous taint" and morals suffer where no political purpose is served. He adds that those absorbed in the rights of man forget man's nature, and that they pervert the sympathies of the human heart (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 114 (edition-specific)).

3. It encourages a spirit of change and contempt for ancient institutions. He says he dislikes revolutions, whose signals have so often been given from pulpits. He ties this to a spirit of change and a contempt for ancient institutions when set against present convenience or inclination (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 46 (edition-specific)).

4. It misreads the English Revolution. He describes the caution of the 1688 settlement as showing a wish to make the Revolution "a parent of settlement, and not a nursery of future revolutions." Men elated by a triumph over oppression are apt to fall into violent and extreme courses (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 49 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not give a fuller theory of when resistance is justified. Burke does allow that extreme occasions may exist, and that revolutionaries may accomplish some good (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 416 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
In the passage provided, Wollstonecraft says gallantry harms women. She calls it "the cold unmeaning intercourse of gallantry" and says it has rendered many women "vain and useless". She sets this against the unhappiness that love has caused some women (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

On society, she calls this "heartless attention to the sex" and says it is reckoned manly and polite. She fears it is a "vestige of gothic manners" that will not disappear until society is very differently organized. She expects a more reasonable and affectionate mode of conduct to be slow to replace it (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

She also says this "lip-service" prevails in the most civilized European states together with extreme dissoluteness of morals, so it has no real moral dignity. Her example is Portugal, where she says it takes the place of the most serious moral obligations. A man is seldom assassinated in a woman's company, but if vengeance cannot be stopped, the lady is asked to pardon the rudeness and depart in peace, even if she is sprinkled with her husband's or brother's blood (Mary Wollstonecraft, A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, Chapter 5, §3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

The other passages do not discuss gallantry directly, so they leave her wider views on the subject unanswered. This account rests on one passage.

detail.answer:
Burke argues that the new French Constitution severs the link between the people and their representatives, and that the Assembly is made sovereign instead of being a trustee for the whole nation.

On the missing connection: he says there is "little, or rather no, connection between the last representative and the first constituent." A member of the National Assembly is "not chosen by the people, nor accountable to them" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific)). He points to three elections, with two sets of magistrates between the member and the primary assembly. This makes the member "an ambassador of a state, and not the representative of the people within a state" (same passage). Burke says that no corrective could change this. Any attempt to reconnect the representative with the primary electors would plunge the state back into the "tumult and confusion of popular election." He concludes that unless the gradation is broken up, the people "do not at all substantially elect to the Assembly" (same passage).

On the structure: he says the scheme tends to split France into independent republics with no constitutional means of coherence or subordination. The only link would be acquiescence in the decisions of a congress of ambassadors, and he says this is what the National Assembly in reality is (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 318 (edition-specific)).

He contrasts this with Britain. There, a representative, separated from the other parts, "can have no action and no existence," and the government is the point of reference for the whole representation. That government is "a trustee for the whole, and not for the parts." In France, by contrast, "the elective Assembly is the sovereign, and the sole sovereign" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 325 (edition-specific)). He therefore calls the French Constitution "the very reverse" of the British in principle (paragraph 326, cited above).

He also doubts that the people's will is served by numbers alone. He says that the will and the interest of the many "must very often differ," and that a government of obscure attorneys and curates would not be good for twenty-four millions even if chosen by many more (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 93 (edition-specific)). He predicts that the Constitution would leave France governed by an "ignoble oligarchy" founded in part on the destruction of the people (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 339 (edition-specific)).
